issues.legal_issue: A directly affected appellant may maintain an appeal and obtain reversal for another party where the challenged judgment proceeds on grounds common to them.
material_facts: The appellant society had been in possession and enjoyment of the fishery before the High Court’s order removed it.
The High Court’s order also impeded the appellant’s application for a later settlement.
The State was a respondent to the appeal and actively supported the appellant.
The challenge to the High Court’s order rested on grounds common to the appellant and the State.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was vitally interested in the matter and could maintain and prosecute the appeal; the judgment could be reversed in favour of the other affected respondent under Order XLI Rules 4 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rules 4 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court may reverse a decree for the benefit of a party where the decree proceeds on a ground common to that party and the appellant. The court applied this principle despite the State not filing a separate appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_adverse_judgment: A party has appealed from a judgment that adversely affects its interests.
predicates.appellant_directly_affected: The appellant was in possession or otherwise directly affected by the judgment and its consequences.
predicates.common_ground_with_other_party: The appellant and another party seek reversal on a ground common to both.

issues.definition: When an adverse judgment directly affects an appellant and rests on a ground common to another party, the appeal may be maintained and reversal may benefit that other party.

issues.legal_issue: A contract made in the exercise of government executive power is unenforceable if it does not satisfy the required formalities for making and executing that contract.
material_facts: The government communicated a decision to settle the fishery rights with the claimant.
The settlement was not made and executed in the prescribed constitutional manner.
issues.conclusion: The settlement was not valid or binding on the government, and the claimant could not base an enforceable claim on it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 299 of the Constitution requires a government contract to be expressly made by the President or Governor, executed on their behalf, and executed by an authorized person and in an authorized manner. Non-compliance makes the contract void and unenforceable. The court relied on State of Bihar v. Karam Chand Thapar & Brothers Ltd., Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India, State of West Bengal v. B. K. Mondal & Sons, and Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh; it noted that estoppel or ratification cannot cure non-compliance.

predicates.government_executive_contract: The agreement was made in the exercise of government executive power.
predicates.required_contract_formalities_not_follow: The agreement was not made and executed in the prescribed manner.

issues.definition: A government executive contract that was not made and executed in the prescribed manner is unenforceable.

issues.legal_issue: A grant of the right to catch and carry away fish must be made through a registered instrument to transfer an enforceable interest in the fishery.
material_facts: The claimed transfer concerned the right to catch and carry away fish, which the court treated as a profit à prendre and immovable property.
The transfer was for a term exceeding one year and reserved yearly rent.
The transfer was not evidenced by a registered instrument.
issues.conclusion: The transfer passed no enforceable title or interest to the claimant.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied sections 54 and 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, and sections 2(6) and 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act. It held that a profit à prendre is immovable property and that the relevant transfer must be registered. It followed Ananda Behera v. State of Orissa.

predicates.fishery_right_transfer: A person purports to transfer the right to catch and carry away fish.
predicates.transfer_requires_registration: The transferred interest is immovable property and the form or duration of the transfer requires registration.
predicates.registered_instrument_absent: The transfer was not made through a registered instrument.

issues.definition: A transfer of fishery rights that requires registration but lacks a registered instrument gives the transferee no enforceable interest.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot be used to enforce an incomplete settlement against the government in the exercise of its sovereign executive functions.
material_facts: The government initially communicated an intention to continue the settlement with the claimant, subject to a deposit.
The claimant made the specified deposit but did not deposit the additional amount required for execution of the lease agreement, and no settlement permit was issued.
The claimant’s allegations that it had invested in boats and entered employment contracts in reliance on the communication were vague and unsupported, and the High Court rejected them.
The government later changed its decision and settled the fishery with the society.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not invoke promissory estoppel to enforce the proposed settlement against the government.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that there can be no estoppel against the government in the exercise of its sovereign legislative and executive functions, applying Excise Commissioner, U.P. v. Ram Kumar. It distinguished Union of India v. Indo-Afghan Agencies Ltd., where the claim concerned an obligation under a government scheme rather than enforcement of a contractual right.

rule.if: government_settlement_action and government_exercising_sovereign_executive_function and settlement_incomplete and reliance_not_proven

predicates.government_settlement_action: The government made and later changed a decision concerning a proposed settlement.
predicates.government_exercising_sovereign_executiv: The government acted in the exercise of its sovereign executive functions.
predicates.settlement_incomplete: The required steps to complete the settlement, such as payment of a required fee or issue of the settlement document, were not completed.
predicates.reliance_not_proven: The claimant did not establish with adequate evidence that it materially changed its position in reliance on the government’s representation.

issues.definition: When the government changes an incomplete proposed settlement while exercising sovereign executive functions, and the claimant does not prove reliance, promissory estoppel cannot enforce the settlement.

issues.legal_issue: Mandamus is unavailable to compel performance of an obligation unless a law imposes a duty and the claimant has a legal right to enforce that duty.
material_facts: The claimant sought an order compelling the authorities to execute the fishery lease and place it in possession.
No statute or rule having the force of law was shown to impose the asserted duty on the authorities.
The asserted obligation arose from the proposed settlement, which was not binding and enforceable.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to mandamus, and the High Court was not competent to issue it.
issues.legal_principle: Mandamus compels performance of public duties prescribed by law. The claimant must show a legal duty imposed by statute and a corresponding legal right to enforce its performance. The court referred to Lekhraj Satramdas Lalvani v. Deputy Custodian-cum-Managing Officer, Dr. Rai Shivendra Bahadur v. Governing Body of Nalanda College, and Dr. Umakant Saran v. State of Bihar.

predicates.mandamus_proceeding: The claimant seeks an order compelling a public authority to perform an act.
predicates.statutory_duty_not_shown: No law imposing the asserted duty on the authority has been established.
predicates.claimant_legal_right_not_shown: The claimant has not established a legal right under that law to enforce performance of the duty.

issues.definition: Mandamus is unavailable when a claimant seeking to compel an authority has shown neither a legally imposed duty nor a corresponding enforceable right.

issues.legal_issue: The government may give preference to an eligible fishermen’s cooperative society when settling fishery rights in accordance with its applicable policy and procedure.
material_facts: A government circular established a revised policy and procedure for settling the fishery.
The policy permitted preference for a fishermen’s cooperative society.
The society’s application for settlement remained pending, and the government’s ability to act was impeded by the High Court’s mandamus.
The court made any settlement with the society conditional on its fulfilling the policy’s requirements.
issues.conclusion: The government was competent to settle the fishery with the society in accordance with the revised policy and procedure if the society fulfilled the stated conditions.
issues.legal_principle: The government may exercise its authority to settle the fishery according to its revised policy and procedure, including by giving preference to a fishermen’s cooperative society. The court referred to the government circular setting out that policy.

predicates.fishery_settlement_proceeding: The government is deciding how to settle rights to a fishery.
predicates.applicable_policy_allows_cooperative_pre: The applicable government policy permits preference for a fishermen’s cooperative society.
predicates.society_fulfills_policy_conditions: The society satisfies the conditions imposed by the applicable policy and procedure.

issues.definition: When a fishery is being settled under a policy that permits cooperative preference, the government may prefer a society that satisfies the policy’s conditions.

issues.legal_issue: A person who paid for a fishery settlement is entitled to a proportionate refund for a period in which the fishery is settled with another society under government policy.
material_facts: The claimant had deposited settlement fees for the relevant year.
The court permitted the government to settle the fishery with the appellant or another fishermen’s society in accordance with the applicable policy and procedure.
The claimant had to maintain accounts for the relevant period under a court order.
issues.conclusion: If the government settled the fishery with the appellant or another fishermen’s society under the policy, it had to refund the claimant the proportionate amount deposited for the relevant period, after examining the accounts.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on section 70 of the Contract Act as the basis for a proportionate refund where the government settled the fishery with a society under its policy. The amount was to be determined after examining the claimant’s accounts.

predicates.settlement_fee_paid: The claimant paid a fee for the fishery settlement.
predicates.government_settles_fishery_with_another_: The government settles the fishery with a society other than the claimant in accordance with its applicable policy.
predicates.accounts_available_for_relevant_period: Accounts are available to determine the claimant’s use of, or entitlement for, the relevant period.

issues.definition: When a claimant paid a settlement fee but the government settles the fishery with another society under policy, the claimant is due a proportionate refund determined from the relevant accounts.
